title: Biomes of the World

cards.h: Climate draws the map of life
cards.b:
A biome is a large community of plants and animals shaped by climate. Temperature and rainfall decide which biome sits where. UPSC asks about forests, grasslands and deserts with their examples, adaptations and threats. It also links to climate change, because biomes are shifting.

The idea comes from Frederic Clements and Victor Shelford in the early 1900s. Remember that a biome is a climate-defined zone, while a habitat is the home of one species.

Land biomes: tropical rainforest, tropical savanna, desert, temperate grassland, Mediterranean scrub, temperate deciduous forest, taiga (boreal forest) and tundra. Moving from the equator to the poles, the temperature falls and the plant forms change from broad-leaf evergreen to needle-leaf to moss and lichen.

Within 10 degrees of the equator. Rain above 2,000 mm, no dry season, 25-27 degrees C. Layers: emergent, canopy, understory, forest floor. Very high diversity, thin soils that leach and lose nutrients. Found in the Amazon, Congo, and Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia). Forest loss through logging, palm oil and cattle is the main threat.

Savanna: grass with scattered trees, wet and dry seasons. East Africa (Serengeti), Brazil's Campos and Llanos. Big herds and predators. Temperate grasslands: fewer trees, cold winters, fertile dark soil. Prairies (North America), Pampas (Argentina), Steppes (Eurasia), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia). These are the world's wheat belts.

Under 250 mm of rain. Hot deserts: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Australian. Cold deserts: Gobi, Patagonia, Ladakh. Plants (xerophytes) have thick stems, waxy leaves, spines, deep roots (cactus, acacia). Animals are nocturnal or store water. Deserts form in the subtropical high pressure belts, in rain shadows (Atacama) and in continental interiors (Gobi).

Mediterranean: hot, dry summer and mild, wet winter, between 30 and 40 degrees on west coasts. Evergreen shrubs, citrus, olive and vines. California, central Chile, southwest Australia, the Cape. Temperate deciduous: four seasons, trees shed leaves (oak, beech, maple). Eastern USA, western Europe, northeast China. Much cleared for farming.

Taiga (boreal forest): the largest land biome, across Canada, Scandinavia and Siberia. Conifers (spruce, fir, pine) with needles that shed snow. Long winters, thin acidic podzol soils, lumber and pulp. Tundra: treeless, permafrost, mosses and lichens, short summer. Arctic tundra stores huge carbon; thawing releases methane and CO2.

No. Warming is pushing the tree line upward in mountains and northward in the Arctic. Rainforest in the Amazon may tip to savanna under drought and deforestation, a possible tipping point discussed by scientists such as Carlos Nobre. Some biologists prefer the term ecoregion because boundaries are fuzzy and local variety matters.

India has rainforest (Western Ghats, northeast, Andaman), savanna-like tropical dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub (Rajasthan, Gujarat), desert (Thar, Ladakh cold desert), mangroves (Sundarbans), and alpine meadows and tundra above the tree line in the Himalaya. Temperate grassland is limited to alpine pastures like the Bugyals of Uttarakhand.

Likely questions: 'Compare savanna and temperate grasslands', 'Why are tropical rainforest soils poor despite lush growth?', 'Impact of climate change on biomes'.

  • Use a table: location, climate, vegetation, soil, human use, threat.
  • Give local names (Pampas, Veld, Steppe) with the continent.
  • For soils: fast nutrient cycling in the plants, not the soil.

o: Nutrients leach away and sit in plants
